title: Calling the name
hook: Namu Amida Butsu in Japan, Namo Amituofo in China

segments.voice: Yesterday, water and ice: still water turning to shining ice, and the ice to a jewel ground. Your line was clear as water.

In a temple in Kyoto, a room full of voices: Namu Amida Butsu. In a temple in Taipei or Singapore, the same name in another tongue: Namo Amituofo. A grandmother says it over her rice. A monk says it as he passes you in a corridor. A man in a hospital bed says it under his breath when the pain comes. The sutra's pictures take patience. This practice can be done by anyone with a voice, or just the breath to whisper. Today's word is the name, said aloud: nembutsu.
screen: `NAMU AMIDA BUTSU.` → `NAMO AMITUOFO.` → `SAID OVER RICE, IN A CORRIDOR, IN A HOSPITAL BED.`

segments.voice: First, the name, which you met in year three with Honen. Namu Amida Butsu and Namo Amituofo are one phrase in two languages. Amida and Amituofo are both Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light. Namu, or namo, is a word of bowing: homage, turning toward, taking refuge. So the whole phrase is a bow, made of sound. Second, the word nembutsu. It's usually rendered as keeping the Buddha in mind. In Pure Land practice, keeping the Buddha in mind came to include saying his name aloud; thinking and saying grew close enough to share a word. Third, the passage that makes this practice so plain. Near the end of the Contemplation Sutra, the Buddha describes a person who has done much wrong in life and comes to the hour of death in fear and pain. A good friend sits beside him and tries to teach him to picture the Buddha, but he can't; he is too pressed by suffering to hold any picture at all. So the friend says, in effect: if you cannot think of him, just say his name. The sutra says he calls the name ten times, and is born in the land of bliss. Fourth, why that matters. The pictures need a steady mind. The name is offered to the person who has none left. Pure Land teachers who put it at the heart of the path point to this passage: it is within reach on the worst day as on the best.
screen: `ONE NAME IN TWO LANGUAGES.` · `NAMU: A BOW. AMIDA: INFINITE LIGHT.` · `IF YOU CANNOT PICTURE HIM, SAY HIS NAME.` · `WITHIN REACH ON THE WORST DAY.` · then, large: `JUST THE NAME.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, say Namu Amida Butsu or Namo Amituofo slowly, once with each out-breath, ten times, aloud or under your breath, counting on your fingers if that helps. If you'd rather not say it, listen to the sound of it in your mind, as a word from a tradition you're visiting. After the tenth, sit quietly with whatever is left.
Nembutsu. Keeping the Buddha in mind, and in Pure Land practice, calling his name: Namu Amida Butsu, Namo Amituofo. Today's word.
Your line: just the name. When the pictures won't come, the name still can. Rest well.

howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists say the nembutsu aloud in temple services, quietly in daily life, and with prayer beads to keep count; Japanese practitioners say Namu Amida Butsu, and Chinese practitioners Namo Amituofo.

chat.says: Why do Pure Land Buddhists just say a name instead of doing harder meditations?
options: The sutra offers the name to someone too pained to picture the Buddha; it's in reach on any day.
The name only counts when a monk says it on your behalf during a temple service.
It's a secret mantra, given only after someone has mastered the picture meditations.
chat.meaning: In the sutra, a dying man too pressed by pain to picture the Buddha is told to just say his name: within reach on the worst day.

Namo Amituofo.meaning: the same name, said in Chinese

Honen.meaning: Japanese monk who taught that calling Amida's name is open to all

notes: The dying person in the lowest grade who cannot hold the Buddha in mind and is told to say the name, ten times, is paraphrased from the sixteenth contemplation (Takakusu, SBE XLIX, 1894); confirm the details and the number ten.
'Nembutsu is usually rendered as keeping the Buddha in mind' and namu/namo as a word of homage/refuge: meanings of the words, not an etymology argument; confirm phrasing.
'For many Pure Land Buddhists, the name is the heart of the path' and 'in many Pure Land communities' is a general claim; soften further if needed.
Hook scenes (greeting in a corridor, said over rice) are illustrative; confirm Amituofo as a passing greeting in Chinese temples is fair to include.
Original 念仏 (Japanese form; Chinese 念佛); pronunciation approximate.
